strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and important leakage channel in locate-then-edit model editing: the parameter update itself can reveal the edited subject subspace. This is a meaningful security/privacy contribution for model editing and open-weight release workflows.

The core subject-inference attack is technically well motivated. The derivation connecting MEMIT/ROME/AlphaEdit updates to the row/right-singular subspace of edited key vectors is clear, and the appendix provides formal guarantees under explicit rank, covariance, and separability assumptions.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for this problem: three LLMs, three editing algorithms, CounterFact and zsRE, batch sizes up to 100, covariance-estimation ablations, and comparisons to a gray-box logit baseline. Subject recovery is consistently strong, often around 0.94-1.00 recall for the white-box attack.
The paper includes a concrete defense, subspace camouflage, rather than stopping at attack demonstration. The defense is analytically characterized and evaluated for utility/protection trade-offs.

The limitations section is unusually relevant and honest: it acknowledges predefined candidate pools, single-step editing, and uncertainty under large-scale continual editing. The impact statement also recognizes dual-use risks.
weaknesses: The threat model is restrictive and drives much of the success. The attacker is assumed to have pre- and post-edit weights, know the editing method and hyperparameters, know or estimate the covariance/projection objects, and search over candidate subject/prompt pools that contain the ground truth. The candidate pools are constructed from the first 2,000 dataset examples, which may substantially overstate real-world recovery feasibility.

Prompt recovery is less convincing than the headline framing suggests. It is template ranking over a fixed prompt library, not open-ended reconstruction, and top-1 recall is modest, especially on zsRE and Qwen2.5. The claim that the attack recovers edited data/semantic context should be qualified accordingly.

The evaluation omits important realistic settings: multi-time/sequential edits are left to future work, larger or out-of-distribution candidate pools are not studied, and there is no evaluation when the edited fact is not drawn from the same benchmark distribution used to construct candidates.

The defense evaluation is mostly against the authors' own KSTER-style subject inference and broad subspace-based arguments. It does not convincingly test adaptive attackers that know the defense, exploit the decoy construction, use residual/value information, combine logits with weights, or attack prompt/object recovery under camouflage.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the abstract says code is available but the link is blank, and several figures render/extract poorly. The appendix gives many implementation details, but the missing code link and incomplete artifact information make independent reproduction harder.

Some theoretical results rely on strong idealized assumptions such as full-rank residual/key matrices and separability of edited versus non-edited key vectors in the candidate pool. These assumptions are plausible in the tested setup but not empirically stress-tested enough to establish general robustness.

strengths: The paper studies a timely and important question: whether locate-then-edit methods for LLMs can leak the edited knowledge through parameter updates. This is a meaningful privacy/security angle on model editing, especially for open-weight model releases or audit settings where pre- and post-edit checkpoints may be compared.

The core subject-inference idea is mathematically natural and clearly connected to the low-rank structure of ROME/MEMIT/AlphaEdit updates. The manuscript gives derivations showing why the update row space can reveal the key-vector subspace under full-rank and separability assumptions.

The empirical scope covers several editing methods, three model families, two standard editing datasets, multiple batch sizes, covariance-estimation ablations, and prompt-template ablations. The reported subject recovery results are consistently strong in the paper's controlled setting.

The paper includes a limitations and impact discussion, and it does acknowledge important restrictions such as reliance on predefined candidate pools and focus on single-step rather than sequential editing.
weaknesses: The main empirical setting is highly constrained and substantially weakens the claimed security significance. The attacker is assumed to have both pre- and post-edit weights, the editing algorithm and hyperparameters, access to the covariance matrix or a good estimate, and a candidate subject/prompt pool that contains the true edited item. In the experiments, subjects are drawn from the first 2,000 examples and the candidate pool is also built from this same slice, which makes the recovery task much more artificial than the framing suggests.

Prompt recovery is only moderately convincing. Top-1 prompt recall is often around 0.5 or lower on CounterFact and much lower on zsRE, with Qwen zsRE top-1 values as low as 0.04 to 0.13 in Table 2. The paper emphasizes top-20 recall and semantic similarity, but exact reconstruction of sensitive context is not reliably demonstrated across settings.

The paper omits object recovery from evaluation, stating that once subject and prompt are recovered the object can be obtained by querying the pre-edit model. This skips a central part of the privacy claim: in realistic settings, recovering the sensitive value is the main harm, and querying the pre-edit model may itself be unavailable, rate-limited, or not yield the intended memorized value.

The proposed defense is not sufficiently validated. It is evaluated mainly against the authors' own subspace-based attack, and the theoretical claims are limited to attacks relying on singular/subspace structure with unknown residuals. There is no convincing evaluation against adaptive attackers, alternative inversion objectives, optimization over candidate keys, or attackers who exploit the decoy construction.

The defense has questionable practicality: it requires constructing decoy key matrices and tuning alpha, and larger alpha values can sharply degrade editing performance, e.g. AlphaEdit on CounterFact drops to 0.46 efficacy at alpha=7 and MEMIT on zsRE drops to 0.59 efficacy at alpha=4. The paper presents this as a manageable tradeoff but does not give a principled deployment criterion.

The theoretical guarantees depend on strong assumptions, especially candidate containment, full-rank residual/key matrices, and separability of edited versus non-edited candidate key vectors. These assumptions are close to the empirical construction and do not establish robustness in open-world or adversarially chosen candidate sets.

Originality is mixed. The row-space analysis is a useful application to locate-then-edit methods, but much of the attack is essentially linear algebra applied to known low-rank closed-form updates, and the defense is a camouflage/decoy subspace construction evaluated in a narrow threat model.

Reproducibility is a serious concern. The abstract says code is available but the URL is blank in the manuscript. Key details such as exact candidate prompt additions, random seeds, checkpoint/configuration versions, and full hyperparameter settings are not sufficient for reliable independent replication from the paper alone.

Presentation quality is below the expected ICML standard. Multiple figures render with corrupted /uni glyph text, making axes, labels, and some visual evidence unreadable. This directly affects the interpretability of important figures such as attention/similarity visualizations and tradeoff plots.

The ethics discussion recognizes dual use but is not adequate for a paper proposing a privacy attack. It does not provide a concrete release plan, safeguards for code/data, or a careful discussion of when publishing the attack and defense details may increase risk for edited open-weight models.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and non-obvious privacy/safety risk in locate-then-edit model editing: parameter updates can act as a side channel for recovering the edited knowledge. This is a meaningful contribution for both model editing and LLM privacy/security.

The attack is technically well motivated. The row-space/key-space analysis for ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit is clean, and the paper provides formal guarantees under explicit assumptions, including robustness to noisy covariance estimates.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: three LLMs, three editing algorithms, CounterFact and zsRE, single-edit and batch-edit settings, and both subject inference and prompt recovery metrics. The subject recovery results are strong, often around 0.94-1.00 recall, and the covariance ablation usefully tests a key assumption.

The paper goes beyond attack demonstration by proposing subspace camouflage as a defense, with both derivations and empirical protection-utility trade-off analyses. This makes the contribution more useful than a vulnerability report alone.

The presentation is generally clear, with good algorithmic descriptions, useful tables/figures, and an honest limitations section acknowledging predefined candidate pools, single-step editing, and uncertain behavior under continual editing.
weaknesses: The threat model is strong and substantially narrows the practical claim. The main attack assumes access to pre- and post-edit weights, the editing algorithm and hyperparameters, covariance/projection information or good estimates, and a candidate subject/prompt library containing the ground truth. This is plausible in some open-weight update scenarios, but not enough to support very broad claims about reconstructing edited data in general.

Prompt recovery is notably weaker than subject recovery. Top-1 prompt recall is often around 0.3-0.6 and can be very low on zsRE for Qwen, while strong top-20 results depend on a 1,000-prompt candidate library that includes the true template. The paper sometimes frames this as recovering semantic context, but exact recovery remains only partially demonstrated.

The defense evaluation is somewhat limited. Subspace camouflage is mainly evaluated against the authors' own KSTER-style subject inference attack, while the theoretical defense claims cover subspace-based attacks under assumptions about unknown residuals. More adaptive attacks, attacks using approximate residual/object information, or attacks combining logits and weights would better establish robustness.

Several theoretical guarantees rely on strong separability, full-rank, and candidate-containment assumptions. These assumptions are stated, which is good, but their empirical validity is only partially probed; the method may degrade when candidate pools are much larger, contain near-duplicate entities, or when edits are sequential and entangled.

Reproducibility is decent but not complete. The appendix gives useful implementation and metric details, but the manuscript's code link appears blank, and some details such as exact editor configurations, hyperparameters inherited from prior work, candidate-pool construction specifics, and random seeds would need to be fully released for reliable replication.

The ethical/impact discussion recognizes dual use, but the work is inherently a capable extraction attack. The paper would benefit from clearer guidance on responsible release, evaluation on genuinely sensitive data surrogates, and concrete mitigations beyond the proposed defense.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful and underexplored privacy/security issue in locate-then-edit model editing: parameter updates can act as a side channel for recovering edited subjects and prompts. This is significant for open-weight release and model-unlearning workflows.

The subject-recovery component is technically well motivated. The derivation that the transformed update row space reveals the edited key subspace for MEMIT/ROME/AlphaEdit is clear, and the appendices provide formal guarantees under explicit assumptions.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad: three LLM families, three editing methods, CounterFact and zsRE, batch sizes up to 100, candidate-pool scaling, covariance-estimation ablations, sequential editing, and defense trade-off experiments.

The results are strong for the main white-box subject inference claim, with top-N recall around 0.94-1.00 across most batch settings and robustness to prompt-template choice and covariance estimation.

The paper includes an honest limitations section and an impact statement acknowledging dual-use risk. The defense evaluation also reports utility and hallucination trade-offs rather than presenting camouflage as free.
weaknesses: The threat model substantially narrows the practical claim. The attacker needs pre- and post-edit weights, the editing algorithm and hyperparameters, access to or estimates of C/P, and candidate subject/prompt pools containing the ground truth. The paper argues these are plausible, but the central recovery results are not prompt-free or open-world recovery.

Prompt recovery is less convincing than subject recovery. Top-1 prompt recall is often modest and zsRE performance is weak for some settings, e.g. Qwen2.5 MEMIT top-1 0.08 and top-20 0.55 at N=100; end-to-end object extraction can be as low as 0.42 top-20 for Llama3-Instruct on zsRE.

The prompt-recovery baseline is weak: choosing the lowest post-edit entropy is very close to the proposed score but omits pre/post entropy change. Stronger baselines such as learned retrieval, paraphrase-expanded prompt search, gradient-free prompt optimization, or attacks using known editing templates would make the evidence more decisive.

The theoretical guarantees rely on strong separability, full-rank, known-candidate, and invertibility assumptions. These assumptions are stated, but the paper does not quantify how often separability fails in realistic candidate distributions or under noisy/merged/released checkpoints.

The defense claims are somewhat overstated. Subspace camouflage is mainly evaluated against the authors' own attack and a simple gray-box baseline, while the theoretical protection covers subspace-based attacks under unknown residuals. Adaptive attackers exploiting residual structure, multiple releases, decoy statistics, or edit-side metadata are not empirically studied.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract says code is available but no URL appears in the manuscript text, and many implementation details defer to prior configurations rather than fully specifying hyperparameters, compute, exact candidate generation, and model-editing settings.

The experiments use standard factual editing benchmarks rather than genuinely sensitive/private data. This is understandable ethically, but it limits how directly the results support claims about recovering memorized sensitive information.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and plausibly important privacy/security question: whether locate-then-edit weight updates leak information about the edited facts. Framing edits as a side channel is a useful perspective for model editing and unlearning work.

The subject-inference attack is technically motivated by the low-rank algebraic structure of ROME/MEMIT/AlphaEdit updates, and the empirical subject-recovery results are consistently strong under the paper's stated white-box assumptions.

The manuscript includes experiments across three model families, multiple edit methods, CounterFact and zsRE, and reports ablations for covariance estimation, candidate pool size, prompt template choice, sequential edits, and a defense trade-off.
The limitations section is candid that the attack relies on predefined candidate pools and that the defense can induce decoy hallucinations or degrade under repeated edits.
weaknesses: The central empirical setup is too artificial to support the paper's broad claims. The attacker is given pre- and post-edit weights, the editing algorithm and hyperparameters, covariance information, and candidate subject/prompt pools guaranteed to contain the targets. In the main setup, edits are sampled from the first 2,000 dataset entries and the candidate subject library is also built from those same first 2,000 entries, making the recovery problem much closer to reranking a curated benchmark pool than reconstructing sensitive data in a realistic open-world setting.

Prompt recovery is especially limited: it is exact-match recovery from a fixed prompt-template library, not reconstruction of arbitrary natural-language edit requests. Top-1 prompt recall is often modest, and zsRE results are weak for some models, e.g. Qwen top-1 around 0.04-0.13 and top-20 around 0.55-0.60 for MEMIT. The paper nevertheless repeatedly states that it recovers “all editing information” or “sensitive data,” which is not justified.

The end-to-end object extraction claim is weaker than advertised. The method obtains the original output by querying the pre-edit model after recovering a subject and prompt, but the threat model already grants access to the pre-edit model. Thus the attack mostly narrows the query/search space; it does not demonstrate recovery when the pre-edit model is unavailable, nor does it isolate leakage attributable solely to the update in a realistic deployment.

The theoretical guarantees rely on assumptions that largely encode the desired separability and idealized rank behavior. Full-rank residual/key assumptions, candidate containment, and separability on the recovered subspace are strong, and the proofs do not address the practical difficulty of open-world candidates, duplicate/near-duplicate subjects, paraphrased relations, or noisy/nonstandard editing pipelines.

Baselines are insufficient. The gray-box JS-divergence baseline is not a strong comparator for a white-box weight-difference attack, and prompt recovery is compared mainly to a naive entropy baseline. The paper does not evaluate natural alternatives such as direct optimization over prompts/subjects, nearest-neighbor search in activation space without the proposed transformation, adaptive attacks against the defense, or attacks with partial/no pre-edit access.

The proposed defense is underdeveloped and evaluated against the authors' own attack. Average rank of true subjects is an indirect protection metric, and the defense introduces semantic decoys that measurably increase hallucination and degrade utility at higher strengths. The claimed broad robustness against subspace-based attacks is not backed by adaptive empirical attacks, and the theory assumes the attacker lacks residual information while the paper's own threat model grants substantial algorithmic knowledge.

Reproducibility is inadequate for an ICML main-track security claim. The abstract says code is available but the manuscript leaves the URL blank. Important details of candidate-pool expansion to millions of subjects/prompts, added prompts, sampling procedures, and implementation of large-scale search are underspecified.

Presentation is generally readable, but it substantially overclaims relative to the evidence. Terms like “recover sensitive data,” “recover all editing information,” and “without original queries” obscure the dependence on curated candidate pools, access to the original model, and benchmark-specific prompt templates.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored privacy failure mode of locate-then-edit methods: the parameter update itself can leak the edited facts. This is significant for model editing as unlearning/privacy tooling and for open-weight model release workflows.

The core subject-recovery attack is technically clean: the paper connects the algebraic form of ROME/MEMIT/AlphaEdit updates to recoverable key subspaces, gives explicit algorithms, and provides theoretical guarantees under stated rank/separability assumptions, including a perturbation analysis for noisy covariance estimates.

The empirical evaluation is broad enough to support the main claim: three LLMs, CounterFact and zsRE, ROME/MEMIT/AlphaEdit, batch sizes up to 100, sequential edits, covariance-source/sample-size ablations, candidate-pool scaling, and comparisons to gray-box/logit baselines. Subject recovery is consistently very strong, often 0.94-1.00 recall.

The paper goes beyond attack demonstration by proposing subspace camouflage, deriving it for multiple editors, and evaluating the protection-utility tradeoff. The defense is not perfect, but it is a useful constructive contribution and highlights practical tensions in securing editing.

The limitations and impact discussion are unusually relevant: the authors acknowledge candidate-pool dependence, decoy hallucinations, and uncertain long-term behavior under large-scale sequential editing, and they discuss dual-use concerns without hiding the security implications.
weaknesses: The threat model is strong. The main attack assumes access to pre- and post-edit weights, the editing algorithm and hyperparameters, covariance/projection information or good estimates, and candidate subject/prompt pools containing the ground truth. The paper argues these are plausible, but the strongest conclusions should be read within this constrained setting.

Prompt recovery is materially weaker than subject recovery. Top-1 recall is often only around 0.3-0.5 on CounterFact and can be very low on zsRE, especially for Qwen; end-to-end original-output recovery is also moderate. Thus the claim of recovering all editing information is somewhat overstated unless top-20/manual verification is acceptable.

The prompt-recovery baseline is relatively weak and the gains over the naive entropy baseline are small for Top-5/Top-20 in several settings. A stronger comparison to prompt-search, paraphrase-generation, or optimization-based prompt attacks would better establish the novelty and necessity of the entropy-ratio method.

The defense evaluation is less complete than the attack evaluation. Subspace camouflage is mainly tested on Llama3-8B-Instruct and against the authors' own attacks or closely related baselines; adaptive attackers that exploit decoy construction, multiple layers, residual/value information, or downstream behavioral probes are not deeply studied.

The defense has nontrivial side effects: increasing camouflage induces hallucinations for decoy subjects and can sharply degrade editing efficacy or specificity at higher alpha values, especially for AlphaEdit and zsRE. The practical operating regime may therefore be narrower than the main narrative suggests.

Reproducibility is only partially demonstrated in the manuscript. The abstract says code is available but the URL appears blank in the provided PDF, and several implementation details needed for exact replication, such as editor hyperparameters, candidate generation procedures, and evaluation prompts, would benefit from clearer central reporting.

Some presentation details reduce polish: figures/tables are dense, several extracted figure labels appear garbled, and important assumptions are distributed across appendices. The paper is understandable overall, but the main text could more directly qualify claims by threat-model and candidate-pool assumptions.
